text:
Animal Welfare and Veganism: Food culture, hunting, pets etc.

I’m beginning to go vegan for ethical reasons regarding animal welfare, and I am increasingly finding the relationship humans have with non-human animals to be disturbing, or at least concerning. Food is such a fundamental part of our lives, and I notice for how much people find a love and passion for it, whether it be in cooking or consumption, people prefer to remain either totally ignorant to its origin, or completely romanticize the process of its acquisition. Even to those who defend acquiring food in a comparatively natural or pastoralistic manner to factory farming are still practicing something that has verifiably demonstrated to cause animals psychological and physical harm. It also makes me question about if having pets is at all adequate at times, when people are sometimes uninterested or possibly incapable of providing adequate to an animal, and their possession is totally to fulfill that desire itself whilst insurance of its quality of life is secondary if a consideration made or fulfilled at all. As to food, the effects, the process of collecting and processing animals solely to consume or commodify them is inconsequential, or it is ceremonialized and worshiped despite in some instances the practical possibility of avoidance or replacement of consumption with alternatives that do not involve animals, their culling, captivity, hunting, or slaughter. The butchering, the hammering, the devouring is a part of the process and continuing to eat without guilt, and perhaps gratitude is the only conceivable option. I realize I have for too long depended on conclusions that prevented me from doing more for non-human animals, and for too long have I done nothing despite having the knowledge and the intuition to recognize that it was wrong and that I am capable of minimizing it, beginning with myself, if not preventing and abolishing it.

text:
Advice needed: How to handle myself better in conversations with non-vegans?

I've been vegan for at least 7 years and have been getting increasingly fed up with the lack of compassion/consideration non-vegans display towards animals. I wouldn't expect people to do a complete 180 overnight and immediately go vegan just because they know a vegan (I certainly didn't), but I'm sick of cutting people slack when I hear the same tired arguments over and over, not to mention seeing people constantly admit they know it's wrong, but don't want to change. 



Anyway, last weekend I was at a wedding and during dinner a conversation came up to do with eating animals. A person at our table said they're fine eating meat because they've worked at a butcher's and in an abattoir and, anyway, they only get meat from locally-grown sources, so it's fine. *(Not an original point, I know...)* At this point, I grumpily snapped something like "But the animal doesn't want to be killed!", which immediately made everything awkward. The other people very quickly left and I later heard them talking to someone else about it. 

 
I clearly went too far and I know I shouldn't have reacted like this\*, it's not that right that my outburst made everyone uncomfortable. I want to be able to respond in conversations like these in a serious, but non-aggressive, manner. Being realistic, I don't expect I'll actually be able to say anything to change people's minds, but I don't want to come across as some crazy vegan.

 
The whole point of this post is I'm looking for suggestions of people I can watch to see examples of people handling themselves in disagreements with non-vegans (I've heard Earthling Ed is a great example of this), so I can handle myself better. Also, if any of you know of any genuinely good responses, which don't make you seem like a complete ass, then I'm all ears for them too. 

 
Tl;dr: How can I better respond in conversations about veganism/eating animals without losing it? Any good resources? 

 

\*The point of this post isn't to do with how we (as vegans) might not like other people (talking about) eating meat or defending it, nor is it about tiptoeing around other people's feelings. Of course, I'm sick of the BS reasons/mental gymnastics people do to avoid confronting the idea that eating animals is wrong, but I need to conduct myself better in conversations like these

text:
Vegan's opinion on vegeterians

Maybe this has been discussed before, but I want to state my own opinion.

I have heard of a lot of repulsion vegans have towards vegetarians recently. There are those who state vegeterians are worse than meat eaters as they are neutral and change sides based on the opportunity presented. Yes, with some unfortunately that is the case, but there are a lot of vegeterians who are in this for the same reason as vegans, yet they are obscured by flexitarians. 

The main problem that occurs when vegans are too stern towards vegetarians is that their opinion, in some cases drives vegeterians back to eating meat (back to the dark side)

My friend is a good example. He was a vegeterian for 2 years and was always seeking for someone who would accept his beliefs, with whom he would have a decent conversation for a change. As he couldn't find those among vegetarians as yeah, they were mostly flexitarians or in temporarily for health reasons, he thought he would find friends in the vegan community.(And not to mention vegeterian communities where all they talk about are vegeterian recepies, never mentioning animals)

Many vegans hated him thinking he does not belong among them as he is not giving all the 100% in. He loves animals and is a big activist against their suffering, but he refuses to be vegan as he states that it's not unethical for him to be a vegeterian. Eventually he lost hope of ever making a diference since neither of the sides were accepting him. You become quite depressed in that case, I would say, as he really wanted to feel accepted among the animal rights activists.

I was in discussions with other vegetarians who felt like him, those who find it ethical to consume milk and eggs if the chickens and cows are treated well. I mean, tell me your own thoughts about that philosophy.

Anyway, not to go too deep in this. What I am trying to say is that vegans rejecting vegetarians is backfiring to the whole vegan community, in my opinion. Because vegeterians would not find enough support and some would go back to eating meat. I know some of you would say: come on just give it a little more effort and become vegan. 

It's true yet there are those who are for example intolerant to soy milk or can't go all the way to become vegan for other justified reasons. I think it's best to give more support to vegeterians and not to be giving them pressure and forcing them prematurely into veganism. As there sure would be those who would eventually become vegans.

Feel free to state your own opinions. I accept anything, even hate towards my view as I am tolerant to any form (after I stopped eating meat I dealt with lots of pressure anyway 😄)

I would just like to see how you guys look at this.

text:
Two Months Vegan

I debated making a follow up post for the last week regarding my first post from the end of July. I was hesitant because I didn't want to just be seen as someone looking for praise for coming to the obvious conclusion about animal rights and ethics. But, I have decided to post to thank this community and to hopefully encourage nonvegans to do the research and make the change.

First I want to thank u/One-Shake-1971 and u/Inside-Weather4033 for commenting on my first post and giving me a jumping off point. After googling what they had posted I started reading "The Case for Animal Rights" by Tom Regan, which I highly recommend. While reading, my algorithm on YouTube started recommending a few vegan friendly videos specifically Dr. Jack Symes Jubilee debate. After watching that video I went vegan the next day. His approach is what sealed the deal for me along with seeing the absurdity of the people he was debating against. Every nonvegan should watch that video in my opinion. 

Secondly I wanted to touch on what that changed looked like for me. For me my food bill was cut in half. I don't buy fake meat very often and I get a lot of my veggies/beans/lentils frozen, canned, or dry. I eat a lot of tofu, which is one of my favorite foods now because of its versatility. I have seen some health benefits already like a loss of some body fat and an increase of energy levels. Honestly the only tough things that I have had to deal with is finding places to eat when traveling and social pressure. Happy Cow has helped a lot with finding restaurants but navigating it with family members has been interesting to say the least...

Thirdly I wanted to thank this community for posting so many positive things here and for providing so many resources in the sidebar. I've watched a few documentaries, including Dominion, and I am currently reading "Animal Liberation Now" by Peter Singer. I have been working my way through that resource cheat sheet, which is an amazing resource for someone new to the movement.

Lastly I wanted to thank Michael from New Mexico who called into "The Line Edge" who started me on this journey. If you see this, you are truly a stand a person and are responsible for making me question my entire world view. Thank you.
label: personal_story

But Not to be dramatic but I feel like I look so much better?? Friends that I haven’t seen in a while I saw yesterday, and they were saying how happy and healthy I looked.

It’s so weird, I genuinely LIKE my face? I looked at myself and thought I looked great. I thought I was cute. I was like, wait, I’m an attractive guy. I have a slightly overweight but muscular build. I have lost no weight at all and have been eating literally whatever I want. But my muscles are more defined, I look better in clothes, I have an actual jawline, I was getting random compliments from strangers.

I’ve struggled with the way I look for as long as I’ve been alive. I have fought a lifelong battle with food. But I think now something’s healing in me psychologically, because I like who I am and what I stand for. That little boy in kindergarten who already feel uneasy and wrong about the world but knew nothing other than how to be kind and gentle. The nine year old who loved the fuck out of his pet hamsters. The middle schooler who sat with the kids who didn’t have any friends, even if it meant he gave up some of his “cool” friends by association. Eating meat genuinely used to freak me out as a kid, I’m not gonna lie. text:
Don't tell me when I became Vegan

Recently, I've reconnected with a friend that is off and on for over 15 years. She invited me to Thanksgiving dinner. At first I declined as she and everyone else we know is an omnivore but she insisted she will make me vegan things and also insists that I bring nothing. She started to describe what she'd make for me and the first words out of her mouth were "cream" and potatoes. I told her I can't have cream and she got even more insistent, "I stayed at your house for months, you think I don't know how to make vegan after that!?" Thing was, back when she crashed with me, I was only a vegetarian. "No you weren't, you were a vegan ever since I met you!" No. I wasn't.

What's bothering me, is how she's trying to tell me it's my memory that is wrong, not hers. As if I would be the one mistaking all the incredibly life-defining moments that brought me to veganism. I can remember bit by bit all the learnings that brought me there, and all the uphill battles I had to take after I went there.

I remember sitting on a public bus wearing a leather jacket and started contemplating how that, because it was skin, it molded around my body so well after wearing it for years. Then suddenly I began to think of how that skin didn't belong to me, that it was once on an animal. I remember the internal debate as I tried to rationalize continuing to wear that jacket in the meanwhile my brain screamed at me visions of the cow it came from. I ended up just, slidding out of that coat, didn't even use my hands to remove it because I talked myself into such disgust of it. Just, like, slithered out of it right there on that public bus. It was a cold day but I never wore that coat from that moment on.

I remember the exact moment I became Vegan. I was lovingly petting my cat when suddenly I imagined what if my cat had to go through what milk cows to through? What if my wonderful little creature has never gotten to experience a loving touch from a person? After that, I went full lifestyle vegan

Almost every single day something happens that would be easier if I was not vegan than that I am. I hate being an outsider to the way everyone around me thinks. Life used to be so easy when I was merely vegetarian. Now, every new social interaction, every purchase I make, all get defined by if it's vegan and cruelty free in one way or another.

The gall. Try to tell me when I became Vegan. No. Vegans and Vegetarians are not the same.

text:
It's silly to avoid white sugar

White sugar is processed with bone char to bleach it. This is a byproduct of factory farming. For this reason, some vegans avoid white sugar even though bone char does not remain in the finished product, and use organic sugar instead.

Bone meal is also a byproduct of factory farming. It is used as a fertiliser to supplement calcium in crops, especially organic crops. It is sometimes used to fertilise organic cane sugar.

In both cases, we're using the same byproduct, so it doesn't make sense to avoid white sugar but eat organic unbleached sugar.

In both cases, if we achieve our goal of eliminating factory farming, we will likely eliminate this byproduct with it.

**All I'm saying is: let's eat Oreos and eliminate factory farming forever.**

Edit: I feel like a lot of top replies are missing my point (or likely just didn't read past the first sentence)

When your response is "Use organic cane sugar" or "use beet sugar", those sources are likely fertilised with bone meal from the exact same source as bone char.

When your response is "Most sugar isn't processed with bone char", then we agree: it's silly to avoid white sugar.

**Edit again: I guess I have to be VERY explicit: white sugar should be labelled vegan. Oreos should be labelled vegan. Organic veggies are vegan. Beet sugar is vegan. All of these things, despite potentially being produced with bone meal or char, are vegan.**

**So stop telling people white sugar isn't vegan.**

text:
Cow tongue gave me bad dreams

I saw this video on twitter of someone cooking a cow's tongue and it made me feel really queasy and disturbed.. I think it's because a recognizable body part has so much more identity than a hunk of vague meat. You can look at a cheeseburger or a steak and say it's just 'meat'.... but when you see a tongue, you're forced to think about how that was a once living thing, tortured, long dead, and now having its body cut up and boiled. Absolutely horrific. The color too. I went to bed pretty soon after and I had this dream where my mother brought this chicken into the house, those nice red and white ones, and they wanted to kill it but they were doing it so wrong. My young sister who can be pretty arrogant was going to do it and she was going to just hack a cleaver into the side of its neck and I was really upset about this and I was really going crazy trying to find a way to fix the situation and they were putting me in the position to have to kill the chicken the right way but of course there is no humane way to kill... I don't know what happened with that vignette but later in the dream the family dog was made of chickpeas and I had to slaughter my dog if I wanted chickpeas (not implying that that's what I did in the dream I wouldn't do that.)

I think this is pretty interesting and revealing about my psychology. I've only been vegan for 3 weeks or so now and I always feel confused and in a way bothered by those who say that animals are not food in any way or that they're super repulsed by meat and stuff... It made me question myself and my own empathy and all. I had a hard time feeling the way I saw others saying they did and I just didn't get it. I'm referring to how people say things that imply it is absurd that a human being in any scenario would ever come to eat an animal or when they have stronger feelings on veganism than I.

I think I'm starting to get that though. When you are vegan and never see eating from an animal as an option, it is so easy and intuitive, it would never cross your mind to eat meat, and it becomes completely ridiculous that someone would do so! Why! It's so easy not to! Death is such a deeply horrifying thing and it weighs heavy that it is so commonplace. It makes someone so inhuman to truly not care. The person who slaughters an animal scares me. The slaughtered animal scares me.

I'm glad this is happening for me because recently I have a hard time with empathy. I can logically understand what beliefs and decisions are most empathetic and good but I very rarely feel emotion surrounding such things.

text:
I Loved Meat… Until I Didn't

Has anyone else transitioned to veganism almost naturally, without really planning to? 
That’s exactly how it happened for me. 
It started with switching from dairy milk to plant-based milk. I never really liked milk anyway, so that was easy. My wife had already been vegan for a few years, but I was still a big meat eater. I mean, I owned two smokers! 😂 
Over time, though, I found myself smoking less and less meat. First, beef just stopped tasting good. Then pork. And eventually, chicken. One day, I came home and told my wife, “Well, I think I’m done eating meat.” And that was pretty much it. 
The only real struggle has been cheese. It’s almost like my mind is still stuck in its old habits. Pizza will sound amazing, and since I’m not a huge fan of vegan cheese, I’ll occasionally convince myself to try regular pizza. But after a couple of bites, I just can’t eat it anymore. It doesn’t upset my stomach or make me sick. There’s just this mental block, and I end up tossing it. 
The benefits have been incredible, though. My blood sugar is back in a healthy range, I’ve lost a significant amount of weight, and I feel so much better overall. 
Now, strangely enough, even my oat milk lattes are starting to lose their appeal. And I LOVE my lattes! 😂 
I’m certainly not complaining. Between the ethical reasons and the health benefits, I feel like I’m exactly where I need to be. What’s fascinating to me is that none of this felt forced. My tastes and desires just gradually changed on their own. 
And I have to laugh because giving something up is a whole lot easier when your body and mind seem to make the decision for you! 😂

I’m curious…has anyone else experienced this? Not necessarily going vegan overnight or making a conscious decision to give everything up, but gradually losing the desire for animal products until one day you realized you just didn’t want them anymore?

I said that, if I ever do go back to eating meat, the first meat I try shall be organic dog meat. I went on about how great deep-fried Pomeranian nuggets are and especially with a Labrador steak. She and the others in the group seemed to be a little confused and grossed out by the idea. No one reacted too strongly, but I think the memo will stick.

One morning I was out to breakfast with my grandmother and she asked if we would split a stack of buttermilk pancakes as usual.

How the narrative that veganism takes an immense amount of effort, or willpower, or social ostracization is quite overdramatized. How the majority of what we eat is built on routine and habit rather than actual necessity, and it only takes a brief moment to break away from it. How easy it is to just say no.

Somehow, while eating that piece of toast, I just knew I would never eat another animal product again. And I was right.

text:
It’s Anthropocentric for Vegans not to be Concerned with Humans

This is a point of tension that often arises on vegan forums: what ethical commitments should vegans have for other humans, and what grounds those commitments?

I have not always been a vegan—I’ve been one for about six years now—but I have always had ethical commitments toward other humans. Now that I am a vegan, however, I have a new reason for my ethical commitments toward other humans. 

Humans are animals, and vegans are ethically committed to justice and liberation for *all animals.* 

Many vegans I have encountered in forums do not see veganism as having to do with humans. Veganism, according to these vegans, is about animals, or non-human animals, but not about humans. 

I understand those with this position may be concerned with human issues taking over vegans’ concern for other animals. I don’t want that to happen either. 

But to claim that humans are excepted from the vegan concern for *all animals* is anthropocentric. It is a form of human exceptionalism that distances ourselves from other animals. It makes vegans seem, and sometimes be, myopic in their pursuit for social justice and it makes many vegans not see various systems of oppression as linked together.

This separation of issues as “human issues” and “animal issues” is harmful to veganism and to the project to create a more just world. We cannot see the suffering of a cow being forced to breed on the one hand, and the suffering of a human woman under patriarchal systems of power that see and treat her as a vessel for reproduction on the other hand, as separated issues ([Carol J. Adams, The Sexual Politics of Meat](https://caroljadams.com/spom-the-book)). They are distinct, yes, but not separate. We cannot see the suffering of the forced disabling of chickens in factory farms from the forced disabling of humans by the US military waste disposal as separated issues ([Sunaura Taylor, Beasts of Burden).] (https://sunaurataylor.net/books/beasts-of-burden-animal-and-disability-liberation/)

Thiskind of anthropocentrism is a harm to animals because humans are animals, and vegans have the power to aid in showing others how the plight of humans is connected to the plight of other animals. 

Why not an intersectional veganism? Why not a veganism that fights for *all animals*?

One of the rescued hens at the sanctuary where I volunteer is a complete asshole. She still deserves to live.

I volunteer at a small farm animal sanctuary on weekends, and there's a hen named Dottie who absolutely cannot stand me.

She pecks at my boots, steals greens from the other hens, and has been picking fights with the same broom for approximately six months. If I refill her water, she acts like I've personally offended her.

Most of the other hens are either friendly or just mind their own business. Dottie apparently wakes up every morning looking for someone to argue with.

Last weekend we had visitors, and she went after someone's shoelace. The woman laughed and said something like, "I thought rescued animals were supposed to be grateful."

She wasn't being mean. I think she was genuinely surprised.

But I've been thinking about that comment ever since.

We spend a lot of time showing people that farm animals are affectionate, intelligent, playful, and capable of forming bonds. And they absolutely are.

But what about the ones that aren't particularly friendly?

Dottie spent the early part of her life being used for eggs. She doesn't owe anyone affection because she's now somewhere safe. Maybe she distrusts humans for perfectly understandable reasons. Maybe she's just a grumpy chicken.

Either way, it doesn't change anything.

I still bring her breakfast. I still clean her enclosure. If she doesn't want me near her, I leave her alone.

I think sometimes we accidentally make animal rights sound like something animals have to earn by being cute or lovable.

Anyway, Dottie is safe, well fed, and continues to hate the broom with every fiber of her tiny body.

text:
the people around me are starting to look different

I’ve been vegan for about 2 years and 5 months now. For the vast start of it, I tried not to let what everyone was participating in around me bother me, though the complete disturbance of it was always in my mind.

But I was able to keep it down. For the most part.

But now, for the past 2-3 months, my disgust towards it has grown so strong that I genuinely can’t keep it down anymore. When I go out to eat with my family I’m disgusted when I even glance at their plates. Because I see everything behind it. I know the truth now. I know the pure terror, fear, torture and absolute horror that’s behind it. I see the being that was put through it. And it’s just right there. On a plate. And the people around me (basically everyone, including my family) are just eating it with joy, saying how good it tastes, like it’s completely normal. It absolutely DISGUSTS me. I genuinely can’t look at them the same anymore. I’m disgusted by everyone who even participates in it, and I’m always so SO baffled that other human beings are just completely fine with the way they’re acting. Enjoying it even. Where’s the empathy? Aren’t humans supposed to be empathetic creatures? It just confuses me. Who even are these people?

And the worst part is my mom just casually talks to me about it too. “We had delicious potatoes and steak last night.” “Oh I think I’ll make some hot dogs tonight.” “Oh yeah I did get new scissors, but they’re more durable and specifically designed for meat!”

When she said that last part, I’m so serious, I legit said out loud at least 5 times that that’s disgusting. She didn’t hear me, but I just couldn’t stop saying it even as I was walking back to the kitchen. My disgust has reached another level. I genuinely can’t take it anymore, and I’ve quite literally have just started to blurt out at people how deplorable it is to me. Though it makes no difference to them. It never does. It leaves me so so confused.

text:
Why is being vegan or vegetarian treated as a political insult in Texas?

The vegan accusations aimed at James Talarico got me wondering: why do some people have such a visceral reaction to vegans and vegetarians? Why is someone’s decision not to eat meat treated as an insult or a reason to think less of them?


If someone wants to reduce their carbon footprint or avoid supporting factory farming, what’s objectionable about that? Plant-based diets generally have a lower environmental footprint, and intensive animal farming can contribute to water contamination from manure runoff, air pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and harm to surrounding ecosystems. Those seem like legitimate concerns, whether or not you personally choose to stop eating meat.


I understand that meat is tied to business interests and cultural traditions in Texas. But should those interests automatically outweigh preserving the environment and limiting pollution? You don’t have to agree with someone’s priorities to respect their choice.
I also don’t buy the argument that individual choices don’t matter because corporations cause far more harm. Holding corporations accountable and taking responsibility for our own choices aren’t mutually exclusive. 

One person isn’t going to solve the whole problem, but why should that make trying pointless or something to ridicule? What happened to “be the change you want to see in the world”?


What I especially don’t understand is the hostility toward people making that choice only for themselves, not lecturing anyone, trying to convert anyone, or telling others what they can eat. Is it about cultural identity, feeling judged even when nobody is judging you, or something else? Why does someone else’s personal food choice provoke such a strong reaction?

400 injured wild animals come through one small LA rescue every year, and almost nobody knows they exist :(

So most wildlife rescues specialize... this bird place, that deer place. turns out there's one in pasadena that just... takes everyone. squirrels, opossums, raccoons, whatever shows up sick or hurt or orphaned. Over 400 wild animals a year come through one small nonprofit hospital, get patched up, and (the whole point) get released back out where they belong... rescue, rehab, release. That's it, that's the mission.

It was founded by an actual licensed wildlife rehabber ( Cleo), and like most places doing the real hands-on work, the animal care eats every waking hour... which means the "telling people you exist" side tends to fall off the edge. And that stuff genuinely matters for a tiny rescue... it's how the donations and the volunteers and the "hey i found an injured bird who do i call" all happen.

So they need someone to take over their monthly newsletter... that's the whole thing. If you can write a warm email and know your way around Mailchimp, you'd basically be the voice that keeps 400 animals a year worth of good work connected to the people who fund it. It's like an hour or two a month, genuinely small, but for a place this size it's the difference between a newsletter going out and just... not

A lovely low-key one if you're a writer who wants to help but can't give a ton of time... small commitment, real impact, and you get to write about baby opossums getting a second chance, which beats most things you could be writing

It's unpaid ofc (small wildlife nonprofit, every dollar goes to the animals)... but if this is your kind of thing, it's a really nice one :)

Anyone who's posted anything vegan online knows the drill... you put something up and within minutes the SAME comments roll in. "The lion eats the gazelle. What difference does one person make. Plants have feelings too."... all the classics... most people either ignore them or get pulled into a fight that goes absolutely nowhere.

Generación Vegana is looking for someone who actually knows how to move in that space. The work is publishing the content they've already put together for you, replying to comments and DMs, and keeping an eye on the conversations building up around each post.

One thing worth saying right away: this role is in **Spanish**. Not "some Spanish helps"... you'd be talking with a Spanish-speaking community every day, so you need to be genuinely comfortable in it and able to read the room on topics that get sensitive fast.

Tbh it's cool bc part of the role is clocking which questions keep coming up, what people actually care about, what lands and what flops... and feeding that back so the next round of content hits harder. You're basically the org's ears in the comment section, which is a weirdly powerful spot to be in.

They give you the content, the key messages and the guidance... everything you need. It's a volunteer role so unpaid, but it's one of those spots where you feel the impact directly because you're the one actually talking to the community :) Runs about 3 to 8 hours a week and you set your own schedule...

text:
there are trillions of wild animals we basically never think about... and almost nobody's fighting for them :(

We talk a LOT about farmed animals (rightly), but there's this whole other category we basically never think about... wild animals. trillions of them, dealing with disease, starvation, injury, disasters, with almost no one in the movement actually working on it. It's lowkey one of the most overlooked corners of animal advocacy and once you notice it you can't un-notice it.

Anywayyy turns out there's an org (Animal Ethics) that's one of the very few actually taking it seriously. They're asking the real questions like "could we vaccinate wild animals, help them through natural disasters, reduce suffering at a scale that's never been possible before." They're genuinely one of the only groups looking at this. 

They also made a documentary digging into where all this is heading.... everyone's being told the future's about to change everything, and almost nobody's asking the obvious question of what it means for animals. The doc actually asks it. Problem is it's basically english-only rn, which for an idea this overlooked feels like such a waste... there's an entire chinese-speaking world that can't get to it yet.

So the ask, i guess... it's not really "a translation gig," it's more like being the reason a whole language's worth of people can finally access this. if you're fluent in chinese + english and you care about this stuff, that's kind of a big deal.

It's **unpaid** ofc.... nonprofit, the whole point is getting the ideas out there, not the budget. but if you've got the languages and the values, it's a meaningful project to put your name on.
